what_it_does: Large internet services are built from 'microservices' — small independent programs (running in isolated containers) that each handle one piece of the work and talk to each other over a network. In a big shared cluster, many containers of the same microservice run in parallel, but they do not all perform equally: some share hardware with noisy neighbors, some get slower CPUs, some experience network hiccups, causing one container to be twice as fast as another at any given moment. Standard load balancers assume all containers are equally fast and spread requests evenly, which means slow containers pile up a backlog while fast ones sit idle — hurting response-time guarantees (called SLAs, or Service Level Agreements) without any way to compensate. This paper argues that instead of fighting this imbalance (for example, by over-provisioning spare capacity), systems should exploit it: continuously measure each container's actual throughput and latency, and dynamically steer more requests toward the faster containers and fewer toward the slower ones. The result is that the cluster extracts more useful work from the same number of machines without needing extra hardware.
